sections.section_title: Electrolysis of Concentrate Sodium Chloride Solution
sections.content_markdown: In concentrated sodium chloride solution, $\text{NaCl}$ becomes ionized and produces $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions. $$\text{NaCl} \longrightarrow \text{Na}^+ + \text{Cl}^-$$ The difference from molten sodium chloride is that the solution contains $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ ions too as water is partially ionized here. $$\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^-$$ During the electrolysis in this electrolytic cell, $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{H}^+$ will go towards the cathode together. We know, $\text{H}^+$ ion is more prone to accept electrons than the $\text{Na}^+$ ion. So, $\text{H}^+$ ion accepts one electron at the cathode and becomes a $\text{H}$ atom. Two $\text{H}$ atoms again join together and become a $\text{H}_2$ molecule. The reaction at the cathode: $$\text{H}^+ + e^- \longrightarrow \text{H} \quad \text{(Reduction reaction)}$$ $$\text{H} + \text{H} \longrightarrow \text{H}_2$$ $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{OH}^-$ go simultaneously towards the anode. We know, $\text{OH}^-$ ion is more prone to donate an electron than $\text{Cl}^-$. However, since the molarity of $\text{Cl}^-$ in the solution is higher than $\text{OH}^-$ ion, so it donates electrons at the anode earlier than $\text{OH}^-$. One $\text{Cl}^-$ ion donates an electron at the anode and becomes a $\text{Cl}$ atom. Two $\text{Cl}$ atoms join together producing a $\text{Cl}_2$ molecule. The reaction at the anode: $$\text{Cl}^- \longrightarrow \text{Cl} + e^- \quad \text{(Oxidation)}$$ $$\text{Cl} + \text{Cl} \longrightarrow \text{Cl}_2$$
